label: Stop 4: The Bourse and the buried river

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: You've reached a big building with columns, lions, and lots of statues, on a square with a wide pedestrian street running past.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: This is the Place de la Bourse, and the building is the Bourse, the old stock exchange.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was built between 1868 and 1873, on the site of a former butter market.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The architect was Léon-Pierre Suys.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: It looks like a palace.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's in an eclectic style, a mix of neo-Renaissance and Second Empire.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You can see the lions at the entrance, by the Jacquet brothers, and figures along the facade symbolizing Art, Agriculture, Industry, and Science.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And inside, the caryatids were carved with the help of a young Auguste Rodin, who worked in Brussels at the time.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Rodin. Here.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: As a young sculptor, working on a commission.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Not the thinker yet.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But what I want to know is about the river.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Right. Turn and look down the long pedestrian street.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That's Boulevard Anspach. And what I want you to imagine is that it's a river.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A river?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Senne. The river that made Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Remember, the name of the city means a home in the marsh.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For centuries, the Senne flowed through the middle of the city, and by the eighteen-hundreds it was a disaster.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: An open sewer, choked with refuse.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It flooded regularly. And it carried cholera.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So they buried it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The reforming mayor Jules Anspach decided to cover it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1865, he chose a design by Léon Suys, the same architect who built the Bourse, to vault the river and build grand boulevards on top.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Between 1867 and 1871, the river was covered.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the boulevard is named after him.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Yes. It's wide, straight, and lined with imposing buildings, modeled on the boulevards of Paris, which Baron Haussmann was building at the same time.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Bourse was the centerpiece.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So we're standing on top of a river.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: We are. It's still down there, in a tunnel, flowing under your feet.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Most visitors never know.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Was it a triumph?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A mixed one. The city got clean water, better health, and a grand new center.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But hundreds of old houses and streets in the working-class neighborhoods along the river were torn down, and whole communities were pushed out.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That's a real cost.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And it's one reason so many people here care about preserving what's left.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What's the boulevard like now?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the twenty-ninth of June 2015, the central boulevards were closed to traffic between the Place de la Bourse and the Place de Brouckère, creating a big pedestrian zone.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's been a place to walk, sit, and have a drink ever since.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: There was a lot of argument about it at first.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Now most people seem to like it.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And inside the Bourse?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The upper floors have housed a museum called Belgian Beer World since September 2023, and the main hall was opened to the public for the first time then.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: If you like beer, it's worth knowing about, and Belgian beer culture was recognised by UNESCO in 2016.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: I'd like to say something about the steps.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Yes. After the attacks of the twenty-second of March, 2016, the steps and the square in front of the Bourse became a place where people came to grieve.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They wrote messages in chalk on the pavement and left candles and flowers.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It became a kind of living memorial, and people still come here to remember.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: It's good to stand quietly for a moment.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It is. This is a place where the city gathers, in good times and in bad.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: So pause here. Look at the building, look down the boulevard, think about the river underneath.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: When you're ready, we have one more stop.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: It's only a few minutes' walk to the west, and it's where the city began.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Head toward the Place Saint-Géry.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You'll find it a short way from the Bourse, in the direction of the old center, among narrow streets and small bars.
